recall_prompt: Say how you would prove 9x² + 24x = 11 — what you add to both sides and why, what you compare with, how you find p, q and y, and how the value of 4/3 + x gives the result.
insider_note: The series starts at the (1/3)² term, so 1 + 1/3 must be added on both sides before any comparison. At the end square 3x + 4 = 3√3, not x = √3 − 4/3 — that choice keeps the numbers whole.

steps.label: Rewrite with factorials
steps.margin_note: First two marks. Each denominator is a product like 5·10·15 = 5³·(1·2·3), so every term becomes (a product)/(k!) times (1/3)ᵏ. The first term (1·3)/(3·6) is the (1/3)² term, so BOTH the 1 and the (1/3) term are missing: add 1 + 1/3 on both sides.
lines: The 1 and the (1/3) terms are missing,

recall.must_convey: That the series is rewritten so the k-th term is a product over k! times (1/3) to the power k, after adding 1 + 1/3 on both sides so the missing early terms are present.
accept: write each term as a product over k factorial times one by three to the power k and add 1 + 1/3 on both sides
split each denominator into three to the power k times k factorial
add 1 + 1/3 to both sides and bring the series to the shape one plus p by one factorial into x by q and so on
prathi term ni k factorial tho, one by three power k tho rayali, rendu sides ki 1 + 1/3 add cheyali
rewrite the denominators as powers of three times factorials

steps.why: The standard expansion of (1 − y)^(−p/q) has a k! in every denominator and a fixed ratio y/q raised to k. Until the given series is written in that exact shape, p, q and y cannot be read off.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to add 1 + 1/3 on both sides when the series starts late, so the comparison has no 1 to match.
Writing 5·10·15 as 5·3! instead of 5³·3! — every factor carries a 3.
Losing the alternating sign when the terms alternate.

steps.label: Compare with the standard expansion
steps.margin_note: Third mark, for WRITING the standard expansion beside the series. The examiner looks for the pattern p, p(p + q), p(p + q)(p + 2q) over 1!, 2!, 3!. All plus signs mean the (1 − y) form.

recall.must_convey: That the series is compared with the expansion of (1 − y) to the power minus p by q, whose coefficients are p, p(p + q), p(p + q)(p + 2q) over 1!, 2!, 3!.
accept: compare with the expansion of (1 − y) to the power minus p by q
match it with one plus p by one factorial into y by q plus p into p plus q by two factorial into y by q squared and so on
use the standard binomial series with negative fractional index (1 − y) to the power minus p by q
(1 − y)^(−p/q) formula tho compare cheyali
the pattern p then p into p plus q over the factorials is the standard series

steps.why: This is the only binomial expansion whose coefficients grow as p, p(p + q), p(p + q)(p + 2q). Naming it turns the rest of the question into reading off three numbers.
common_mistakes: Using the (1 − x) form for an alternating series or the (1 + x) form for an all-plus series.
Writing p(p + 1) instead of p(p + q) — the step between factors is q, not 1.

steps.label: Find p, q and y
steps.margin_note: Fourth and fifth marks. p is the first factor (1), p + q is the second (3) so q = 2, and y/q equals the common ratio 1/3 so y = q/3 = 2/3.

recall.must_convey: That p = 1 and p + q = 3 give q = 2, and y/q = 1/3 gives y = two by three.
accept: p is one, p plus q is three so q is two, and y by q is one by three so y is two by three
the first factor gives p equal to one and the second gives q equal to two
y by q equals one by three so y equals two by three
p one, q two vasthai, y by q one by three kabatti y two by three
read off p from the first numerator and q from the gap between the factors

steps.why: Three unknowns need three matches: the first numerator fixes p, the second fixes p + q, and the ratio inside the bracket fixes y/q. Nothing else in the series is free.
common_mistakes: Taking y = 1/3 directly — the bracket holds y/q, so y = q × 1/3.
Reading q from the second factor as a whole instead of as p + q.

steps.label: Evaluate the power
steps.margin_note: Sixth mark. Substitute p, q, y into (1 − y)^(−p/q) and simplify the fraction inside the bracket before touching the exponent.

recall.must_convey: That substituting gives four by three plus x equals root three.
accept: substituting gives four by three plus x equals root three
put the values into (1 − y)^(−p/q) and simplify to get four by three plus x equals root three
the bracket becomes one by three and the power gives four by three plus x equals root three
values substitute cheste four by three plus x equals root three vasthundi
simplify the bracket first then apply the negative index
heard_as: four by three plus x equals root three

steps.why: A negative index inverts the fraction and a fractional index takes a root. Doing the inversion first keeps the root over a simple fraction.
common_mistakes: Inverting the exponent instead of the fraction when the index is negative.
Leaving a root in the denominator without a clear final value.

steps.label: Rearrange and square
steps.margin_note: Seventh mark. Clear the fraction first: 3x + 4 = 3√3. Squaring THAT keeps the numbers whole; squaring x = √3 − 4/3 does not.

recall.must_convey: That 4/3 + x = √3 gives 3x + 4 = 3√3, and squaring gives 9x² + 24x + 16 = 27, so 9x² + 24x = 11.
accept: four by three plus x is root three so three x plus four is three root three and squaring gives nine x squared plus twenty four x plus sixteen is twenty seven
multiply by three then square to get nine x squared plus twenty four x equals eleven
three x plus four equals three root three, square it, sixteen goes across and eleven is left
three x plus four ni square cheste twenty seven vasthundi, sixteen subtract cheste eleven
squaring three x plus four gives the result eleven

steps.why: Multiplying by 3 before squaring turns every coefficient into a whole number, which is exactly the 9x² + 24x the question names.
common_mistakes: Squaring x = √3 − 4/3 term by term, which makes the fractions much harder.
Forgetting that 1 + 1/3 = 4/3 was added, and writing x = √3.
